title: Dream of the Red Chamber
subtitle: Seeking Ancient Traces in Grand View Garden · Red Walls and Azure Tiles Recall the Dream
description: Dream of the Red Chamber is the pinnacle of classical Chinese fiction. With the brush of "concealing true facts beneath rustic speech," Cao Xueqin wrote of all the splendor and disillusionment of the mortal world within the fictitious Jia Mansion and Grand View Garden. Yet it was not conjured entirely from nothing — the pavilions and terraces of Grand View Garden, the ancestral hall and family temple of the Jia clan, the swirling incense smoke of Qingxu Temple — all are deeply rooted in the real architectural spaces of eighteenth-century China. This trail follows the footsteps of Baoyu and Daiyu, visiting every setting mentioned in the novel — from the Forbidden City's imperial majesty to Suzhou's private gardens, from Qufu's Confucian Temple and clan hall to Nanjing's ruined relics. Across nationally protected heritage sites spanning six provinces and municipalities, we fully restore the true prototypes of the Dream of the Red Chamber's dreamscape.

route.title: Dream of the Red Chamber: In Search of Grand View Garden Among National Heritage Sites
route.intro:
Pages full of idle words, a handful of bitter tears.
During the Qianlong reign, in Yellow Leaf Village west of Beijing, a fallen banner man named Cao Xueqin was writing a book destined to change the course of Chinese literature. His great-grandmother had been the Kangxi Emperor's wet nurse; his grandfather Cao Yin was Textile Commissioner of Jiangning, the Kangxi Emperor's confidant and cultural agent. The Cao family held the Imperial Textile Mills in Nanjing, Yangzhou, and Suzhou for nearly sixty years, hosting four of the Kangxi Emperor's six southern tours. And then — the house was raided. Overnight, an existence of bell-ringing and cauldron-eating vanished into nothing. The young Cao Xueqin was cast out of Jinling's warm nest of luxury into the smoke and fire of Beijing's common streets. Years later, in a tiny hut at the foot of Fragrant Hill, gnawing on cold flatbread, he sketched stroke by stroke the pavilions and chambers he could never return to, the people he would never see again. He wove those real architectural spaces — the stern majesty of the Forbidden City's inner courts, the sprawling mansions of Prince Gong's Mansion, the waterside pavilions and winding corridors of the Humble Administrator's Garden, the ritual halls of the Confucius Temple, the incense-burners and bells of White Cloud Temple — into a fictional "Grand View Garden." But this fiction bears the shadow of truth at every turn. Every winding corridor and angled path, every waterside pavilion and terraced kiosk finds its corresponding prototype among the surviving national key cultural heritage sites. This trail moves chapter by chapter, scene by scene — from the Illusory Land of Great Void to the ruins of Jinling — completing a full investigation of every real-world architectural setting reflected in Dream of the Red Chamber.

stops.title: Chapter One: The Illusory Land of Great Void · The Dream Begins
stops.content: From its very first chapter, Dream of the Red Chamber is not a book of this world. In Chapter One, Nüwa mends the heavens and leaves a single stone unused, abandoned at the foot of Blue Ridge Peak on Great Waste Mountain beyond all boundaries. A Buddhist monk and a Taoist priest transform it into a fine piece of jade, to be taken to "a prosperous, enlightened nation, a family of poets and officials, a place of flowers and willows, warmth and luxury, romance and wealth" for a taste of mortal life. The master of this stone — the Divine Attendant in Waiting — watered a Crimson Pearl Plant on the banks of the Spirit River with sweet dew. The plant later cultivated a human form, vowing to repay his kindness with a lifetime of tears. The Divine Attendant descended to be reborn as Jia Baoyu. The Crimson Pearl Plant became Lin Daiyu. In the real world nearby, the Suzhou scholar Zhen Shiyin, a mere onlooker, lived on Benevolence Lane, Ten Mile Street, outside Changmen. Next door was Gourd Temple — a tiny shrine whose frying oils caught fire, burning the entire street to the ground. In that conflagration, Zhen Shiyin lost his daughter Yinglian and his fortune, then drifted away with the monk and the priest. Gourd Temple itself was unremarkable, but for "small temples amid the mortal dust," remnants are everywhere south of the Yangtze. By West Lake in Hangzhou, the Lingyin Temple Stone Pagodas and Sutra Pillars — Five Dynasties pagodas and sutra pillars nestled among the lush trees of Peak That Flew Here — embody precisely the spatial archetype of Gourd Temple: small temple with thriving incense, its gate thronged with peddlers, porters, and neighbors. When the fire came, the whole street was doomed. Chapter Five goes even further. Baoyu, napping in Qin Keqing's chamber, dreams his way into a place called the Illusory Land of Great Void. There he finds the Department of Infatuation, the Department of Resentment, the Department of Dawn Weeping, the Department of Night Sorrow, the Department of Spring Sentiment, the Department of Autumn Grief — and there he reads the fates of the Twelve Beauties of Jinling, both the main register and the supplementary ones, and listens to fourteen celestial songs. "Who are the seeds of love? Only those for whom wind and moon are deep." Where did the Illusory Land of Great Void find its prototype? It is not an earthly building, yet it undoubtedly borrowed the spatial imagery of the highest earthly architecture — the Forbidden City. The supreme presence of the Hall of Supreme Harmony, the deep seclusion of the Palace of Heavenly Purity, those tiered halls beneath layered eaves — Cao Xueqin transplanted the spatial sense of the imperial palace wholesale into the dwelling of Fairy Disenchantment. Especially the description of "a five-bay main gate with round-tile roof ridges — side chambers, deer-eaved corner rooms, connected in all directions, lofty and magnificent" — which nearly perfectly matches the spatial sequence of the Forbidden City's first three great halls. And standing at Beijing's highest point, atop the Ten Thousand Spring Pavilion on Jingshan Hill, overlooking the full panoramic sweep of the Forbidden City — the golden glazed tiles spreading like a billowing tide from your feet to the horizon — you grasp the metaphor of "Thousand Red Caves" and "Ten Thousand Beauties' Cup." That is not tea and wine. It is an entire city, an entire dynasty's prime, compressed into a single dream. Jingshan was the imperial rear garden in the Yuan and Ming dynasties; it was at the foot of Jingshan's eastern slope, on an old locust tree, that the Ming Chongzhen Emperor hanged himself — a realm and a dream, completing their final ritual on this small man-made hill.
stops.poem:
On Great Waste's Ridge beyond all mortal ken,
Divine Attendant's dew brought love to men.
Though the Illusory Realm be halls of air,
Each tile bears Forbidden City's dragon-scroll there.

buildings.n: Lingyin Temple Stone Pagoda and Scriptures

stops.title: Chapter Two: The Imperial Consort's Homecoming · Grand View Garden Rises
stops.content: The most magnificent scene in Dream of the Red Chamber unfolds across Chapters Seventeen and Eighteen. Jia Zheng's eldest daughter Yuanchun, after years within the palace walls, receives news: by imperial grace, consorts may return home for a family visit. To welcome this noble lady emerging from the deep walls of the Forbidden City, the Jia clan exhausts its full strength, merging the Garden of Assembled Fragrance from the Ningguo Mansion with the eastern compound of the Rongguo Mansion, expanding three and a half li in every direction — building a garden where "all the sights of heaven and earth were assembled": the Grand View Garden. On the day of the homecoming visit, Yuanchun speaks her first line: "In a humble farmer's home, though one eats pickled vegetables and wears homespun cloth, one can still enjoy family reunion. Now, though we have reached the utmost wealth and honor, our flesh-and-blood are scattered — in the end, where is the pleasure?" And she weeps. The jarring contrast of this scene is so powerful precisely because its stage is genuine imperial space — the Forbidden City. Nine hundred and ninety-nine and a half rooms, thirty thousand square meters of plazas, seventy-two hectares of forbidden precincts — no matter how wealthy you may be among the people, standing beneath the gates of this city, you are small as dust. Yuanchun was not being polite in her palanquin; she knew too well the temperature difference inside and outside those red walls. As for Grand View Garden's own spatial prototype, scholars agree that none matches Prince Gong's Mansion and Garden more closely. The residence of the Qianlong-era powerful minister Heshen, later the home of Prince Gong Yixin — "one Prince Gong Mansion, half a dynasty's history." The mansion itself has three central axes, seven courtyards deep, with a garden of nearly forty mu, complete with hills and water. The "Dripping Emerald Cliff" Taihu limestone rockery in the western garden can nearly be mapped one-to-one with Baoyu's inscribed phrase "a winding path leads to a secluded spot." The garden's scale — neither the vast remoteness of imperial grounds nor the cramped confines of ordinary officials — is precisely the scale of Grand View Garden: traces of imperial ritual in its most important spaces (Yuanchun's Resplendent Villa) and the intimate charm of a private garden at its key points (the twists of Happy Red Court, the deep seclusion of Bamboo Lodge). Imperial garden aesthetics are also in Grand View Garden's blood. At the Summer Palace — Kunming Lake shimmering, Longevity Hill's Tower of Buddhist Incense commanding the whole, the seven-hundred-twenty-eight-meter Long Corridor linking hundreds of pavilions — "embracing hills and encircling waters, built with consummate skill." The spatial layout of Grand View Garden, with its scattered compounds around a central lake, takes as its skeleton the one-lake-three-island model. And older still, the Beihai Park and Circular City — the white dagoba on Jade Flower Island rising high, lakeside pavilions spaced with perfect rhythm — is the very progenitor of this garden pattern. A detached palace was built here in the Jin dynasty; under the Yuan, Jade Flower Island became the center of the Great Capital's imperial city. Five centuries of cultivation yielded this landscape of light and shadow. The axial arrangement of the Resplendent Villa with scattered lodges along the lakeside is the literary expression of this tradition. And there is another layer that must be discussed — ritual. An imperial consort's homecoming is a state ceremony, not an ordinary family visit. At the Temple of Heaven, the Hall of Prayer for Good Harvests, with its triple eaves and azure glazed-tile cone, the Circular Mound Altar with its eighty-one concentric stones — this ritual scale forms the foundation of the ceremonial space of Grand View Garden's Resplendent Villa. When Yuanchun entered the garden, eunuchs cleared the way, palace lanterns lined the route, she changed robes, ascended the dais to receive obeisance — the solemnity of these procedures is in direct lineage from the Heaven-worshipping rites of the Temple of Heaven. And the Zhengyang Gate — Beijing's central southern gate on the city's axis — its tower soaring high, its arrow tower imposing. In those days, when the emperor went on tour or the consort returned home, they had to pass through this gate. Yuanchun's palanquin, passing through the bustling traffic "beyond Zhengyang Gate" on its way to the Jia mansion — this is the capital's coordinate that appears fleetingly within the novel. When the homecoming ended, "the eunuch-in-charge announced: 'The hour is chou-zheng-san-ke — the imperial carriage should return.'" Chou-zheng-san-ke: 2:45 in the morning. The most glorious night of Grand View Garden ended in the cold wind before dawn. Yuanchun turned for one last look as she boarded her palanquin — that garden where she had spent only a few hours would be the Jia family's last splendor.
stops.poem:
By royal grace the garden rose to greet the phoenix throne,
Prince Gong's old mansion set the scale in wood and stone.
Ten thousand acres of imperial parks and halls
Became the Grand View Mountain of the Red Chamber's walls.

stops.title: Chapter Three: Days in the Garden (Part One) · Burying Flowers and Forming a Poetry Club
stops.content: After Yuanchun left, Grand View Garden did not go empty — it grew livelier. She issued an edict: let Baoyu and all the young ladies move in. So Baochai took Alpinia Park, Daiyu took Bamboo Lodge, Yingchun took Embroidery Tower, Tanchun took Autumn Freshness Studio, Xichun took Lotus Maze Pavilion, Li Wan took Paddy-Sweet Cottage, and Baoyu took Happy Red Court. The garden had become a home. The most beautiful passages in Dream of the Red Chamber — Daiyu burying fallen blossoms, Baochai chasing a butterfly, Xiangyun drunk asleep on a peony bed — all unfold within this garden. Cao Xueqin describes each courtyard's scenery with extraordinary precision: Bamboo Lodge "with a phoenix-tail density of bamboos, the rustling of a slender dragon's song — a thousand emerald canes screening the view"; Alpinia Park "not a single flower or tree, but countless strange herbs... trailing vines, hanging from peak to crag, dripping down to eaves and pillars, winding around steps and railings"; Happy Red Court "with a few rocks set in the courtyard, a banana tree on one side, and on the other a Xifu crabapple whose canopy spread like an umbrella, silken green tassels trailing, vermilion stamens spitting cinnabar." These lines read like a garden guidebook — because Cao Xueqin was indeed "writing about gardens." As a child he spent considerable time with his grandfather Cao Yin in Suzhou, and Suzhou's garden DNA was deeply planted in his sensory memory. At the Humble Administrator's Garden, Suzhou's largest surviving classical garden, water is the center — broad ponds with lush groves. In the central garden, the Fragrant Snow Pavilion is open on all four sides; every window frames a landscape painting. Does this remind you of the "carved, openwork sandalwood partitions" in Happy Red Court? Baoyu's room, with its clouds and cranes, Three Friends of Winter, landscapes and figures — layers of space carved out by wooden screens — is precisely the interiorization of the Humble Administrator's Garden's everywhere-visible "framed-view" technique. The Lingering Garden is famed for its masterful spatial handling. From the oppressive narrowness of the entrance passage to the sudden openness of the central garden, then to the deep courtyard turns of the eastern section — "suppress first, then release, layer upon layer." When Jia Zheng led the party through Grand View Garden in Chapter Seventeen, a green screen hill blocked their view at the entrance. As everyone exclaimed "Fine hill! Fine hill!" Jia Zheng said: "Without this hill, the whole garden would be visible at one glance — where would be the interest?" This is the Lingering Garden's entrance philosophy: never let the visitor see through at once; one must go around to discover a hidden world beyond. The Master-of-Nets Garden — half a hectare of exquisite miniaturization — was hailed by Chen Congzhou as "the supreme example of the small garden." Its quality of being "small yet complete, refined yet deep" is precisely the soul of Daiyu's Bamboo Lodge. Just two tiny retiring rooms, a few hundred bamboos screening the view, a single winding covered walkway — the space could not be smaller, yet it is so secluded that once inside, you never want to leave. Here Daiyu read, wrote poetry, daydreamed, wept — such a tiny courtyard and such immense solitude forming an exquisitely poetic tension. The Master-of-Nets Garden's "Bright Hall" wing, replicated at New York's Metropolitan Museum of Art in 1980, allowed the West to feel for the first time what it means to say "without entering a garden, how could spring be such?" The rockery labyrinth of the Lion Forest Garden is even more wonderful — built by disciples of the Yuan-dynasty Chan master Weize, the piled stones seem like a pride of lions crouching, caves and ravines so deep one can get lost. Both Kangxi and Qianlong were captivated by it; Qianlong even had a replica built at the Chengde Mountain Resort. Baoyu and the girls loved darting through the rockeries, chasing each other in the garden — that wild playfulness of threading through stone crevices is one with Lion Forest. And then there is the Mountain Villa with Embracing Beauty — barely three mu in area, yet the Taihu limestone mountain piled by the great Qing-dynasty rockery master Ge Yuliang contains a thousand peaks and myriad ravines, a deep grotto world recognized as the apex of Chinese garden rockery art. The entrance rockery in Grand View Garden — "white rocks towering, some like demons, some like wild beasts, standing in a dense, defiant cluster, covered with moss and draped with creepers, a narrow sheep-track barely visible" — is precisely the Mountain Villa technique of shrinking a thousand-li landscape into a single square foot. Within these gardens, Daiyu buries flowers, Baochai chases butterflies, Xiangyun sleeps drunk — those immortal literary moments were all born of real garden aesthetics.
stops.poem:
Bamboo shadows in Bamboo Lodge beneath the half-lit moon,
Alpinia Park's strange herbs breathe a fragrant boon.
Six centuries of Suzhou gardens still abide —
The very land where Bao and Dai once walked side by side.

stops.title: Chapter Four: Days in the Garden (Part Two) · Granny Liu's Garden Tour
stops.content: If Grand View Garden's refinement had consisted only of the young ladies' and masters' poetry and song, it would have been too thin. Cao Xueqin introduced a stroke of genius — letting an old countrywoman bring the garden down to earth. In Chapters Thirty-Nine through Forty-Two, Granny Liu pays her second visit to the Rongguo Mansion. This old village woman brings fresh-picked fruits and vegetables to see her benefactors in the Jia household. The Lady Dowager is so delighted that she keeps her for two or three days and takes her on a full tour of Grand View Garden. Thus are born the most humorous, the most vivid, the most spatially aware chapters in the entire book — a complete traversal of Grand View Garden through the eyes of an old countrywoman. They first reach Bamboo Lodge. Daiyu's room — "by the window, on the desk, brush and inkstone; on the bookshelves, piles and piles of books" — Granny Liu mistakes it for a young gentleman's study. The Lady Dowager laughs: "This is my granddaughter's room." Granny Liu sizes up Daiyu and says: "This doesn't look like a young lady's boudoir at all — it's finer than the finest study." An illiterate old countrywoman, in the plainest of words, speaks the essence of the Jiangnan literati garden: the garden is the study, the study is the garden. This is precisely the spirit of the Garden of Cultivation — the private garden of Wen Zhengming's great-grandson Wen Zhenmeng, Ming dynasty. Spacious and unadorned, brimming with bookish elegance, a single pond with a few flowers and trees — no carved beams or painted rafters, only the innate refinement of the scholar. This attitude — "a garden's greatness lies not in size but in character" — is precisely the spatial keynote of the gifted young women of Grand View Garden. The Lady Dowager hosts a feast for Granny Liu, moving from Autumn Freshness Studio to Alpinia Park and then to Lotus Fragrance Pavilion. Along the way Xifeng teases Granny Liu with golden chopsticks for pigeon eggs. Granny Liu stands up and booms: "Old Liu, Old Liu, my appetite is big as an ox — I can eat a whole sow without looking up!" The entire table collapses with laughter: Xiangyun spits out her rice, Daiyu laughs herself into a coughing fit, Baoyu rolls into the Lady Dowager's lap. After the feast they tour the garden, arriving at Baochai's Alpinia Park — "like a snow cave, not a single ornament, only a clay vase on the desk holding a few sprays of chrysanthemum, two books, and a tea set." The contrast between inside and outside is enormous: outside, strange herbs and immortal vines fill the air with fragrance; inside, it is as bare and plain as a snow cave. Baochai's Alpinia Park and Daiyu's Bamboo Lodge — one stark and one elegant, one cold and one secluded — echo perfectly the paired east-west gardens of the Couple's Retreat Garden, whose design theme is "husband and wife as a pair." And in Grand View Garden, the twin peaks of Baochai and Daiyu — one favoring an extreme cave-like bareness, the other a deep-secluded bamboo grove — form a wonderful spatial symmetry. But gardens are not only in Suzhou. The Yu Garden in Shanghai's old city — built in the Ming Jiajing reign by Pan Yunduan to "please his aged parents" — also has rockeries by the master Zhang Nanyang. The great rockery stands about fourteen meters high, its piled-stone technique showing not a trace of chisel marks, relying purely on natural texture. In Yangzhou, two celebrated gardens: the Garden of Individuality, using four colors of stone to create the four seasons — spring hills of bamboo-shoot stone, summer hills of cloud-like lake stone, autumn hills of yellow stone cliffs, winter hills of white xuan stone — the very idea of manufacturing seasonal change within a single garden echoes Grand View Garden's technique of giving each courtyard a distinct character through its plantings. The He Garden, also called Jixiao Mountain Villa, is famed for its fifteen-hundred-meter two-story covered corridor — a double-decker gallery linking every pavilion like a ribbon — which calls to mind the long winding corridors and paths connecting all the courtyards of Grand View Garden. Before Granny Liu leaves, Xifeng asks her to name her child. Learning the child was born on the seventh day of the seventh month, Granny Liu names her Qiaojie — "meeting what is clever" — saying "fight poison with poison, fight fire with fire." It is one of the most tender moments in the book: an old countrywoman, with the most rustic folk wisdom, gives a name to the youngest child of the Jia family. Grand View Garden is not merely a place of wind and moonlight — in Granny Liu's coarse tea bowl, in the pumpkins and dried eggplants she brought, in the pigeon egg that burst with grease when she bit into it — the garden touched the earth.
stops.poem:
The country crone brought melon-scent to the garden's gate,
Xifeng teased her with golden chopsticks — oh what a fate!
Yu Garden's rocks and Yangzhou's winding ways
Are not so cool as Alpinia Park's snowy haze.

stops.title: Chapter Five: The Jia Clan's Ancestral Rites · Ritual Under Heaven
stops.content: If the consort's homecoming was the Jia family's "state ritual," then the New Year's Eve ancestral sacrifice in Chapter Fifty-Three was their "family ritual." "The Jia family members were arranged in the zhaomu order of generations, lining up in their ranks. Jia Jing presided, Jia She assisted, Jia Zhen offered the wine vessel, Jia Lian and Jia Cong offered silk, Baoyu presented incense, Jia Chang and Jia Ling spread the kneeling mats and guarded the fire basin. In blue robes the musicians played; three times the wine was offered, the rites performed; the ceremony ended, the music stopped, and all withdrew." Every detail of this passage — the zhaomu generational division, the three wine offerings, the burning of silk — is authentic traditional clan sacrificial ritual. The highest-standard sacrificial ceremony in all of China is not in the Jia mansion but in Qufu, Shandong — the Qufu Confucius Temple and Kong Family Mansion. The Hall of Great Perfection, nine bays wide with double-eaved hip-and-gable roof, its ten front columns deeply carved with coiling dragons sporting among clouds — two dragons to a column, stirring seas and heavens. The Forbidden City's Hall of Supreme Harmony has dragon columns of royal majesty; Qufu's Confucius Temple has dragon columns of scholarly faith — finer, more exquisite, bearing the pride of "culture is here." Annually, in the spring and autumn months, the Duke of Yansheng presides over the grand Confucian memorial ceremony — bells and chimes sound, ritual conductors chant, attendants bear wine vessels. The entire ceremony of "Jia Jing presiding, Jia She assisting, Jia Zhen offering the wine vessel" at the Jia ancestral hall is a reduced replica of Qufu's Confucian sacrifice. The plaque in the ancestral hall reads: "Carefully attend to the end and pursue the distant past" — from the Analects, the very soul of Confucian ethics. Gazing up at the Kangxi Emperor's inscription "Teacher of Ten Thousand Generations," the Yongzheng Emperor's "Unprecedented Among the People," and the Qianlong Emperor's "Joined with Heaven and Earth" in the Hall of Great Perfection — you understand why the Jia family valued sacrifice above life itself. They were not worshiping spirits; they were sustaining the foundation of order. And the Confucius Forest allows this order to transcend time — an unbroken family cemetery spanning two thousand five hundred years, over a hundred thousand tombs, with strict generational hierarchy and zhaomu order — the longest continuously surviving family burial ground in the world. When the Lady Dowager, with the entire clan young and old, kowtowed before the ancestral tablets, what she bowed to was this river of bloodline. "The Jia Clan Ancestral Hall" — a fictional shrine — was given its narrative weight by the very real presence of the Qufu Confucius Temple and Confucius Forest. Geographically closer to the Jia family's "capital" coordinates are several imperial ritual buildings within Beijing. The Temple of历代 Emperors — where Ming and Qing emperors offered sacrifice to successive dynastic rulers and their meritorious ministers, with the Qianlong Emperor's personally inscribed plaque "Report Achievements, Observe Virtue," enshrining the worldview that "the Chinese imperial lineage is an unbroken thread." If the Qufu Confucius Temple is a "family rite," the Temple of历代 Emperors is a "state rite" — the ritual nature of the Jia family ancestral sacrifice embeds the rise and fall of one family into the grand narrative of "family and state as one structure." And the Imperial Ancestral Temple — the supreme ritual building where Ming and Qing emperors sacrificed to their ancestors, three courtyards, three halls front to back, yellow glazed tiles with double-eaved hip-and-gable roofs. The emperor performed ancestral rites here every New Year's Eve and Winter Solstice — on a scale dwarfing anything the Jia family could muster. What was the Jia ancestral hall? It was a scaled-down spiritual imitation of this Imperial Ancestral Temple by a "power-holding family." And at the other end of the central axis, the Altar of Land and Grain — a square altar paved with the five-colored soils of the realm — represents the state itself. Here the emperor prayed for bountiful harvests and peace under heaven. When the Jia family performed their ancestral rites, what were they praying for? For flourishing descendants and eternal official honors. Interestingly, Cao Xueqin placed this sacrificial ceremony in Chapter Fifty-Three — the exact midpoint of the novel. After this, the Jia family would never celebrate another New Year again.
stops.poem:
The Jia ancestral hall in candle-shadows deep,
In Kong Forest pines and cedars the ages weep.
"Carefully attend the end" — the Temple's call,
Imperial Ancestral Temple's ash now covers all.

buildings.n: Qufu Confucius Temple and Confucius Mansion

stops.title: Chapter Six: Qin Keqing's Funeral · Through the Iron Threshold
stops.content: The Jia family's first grand ceremony was a funeral. In Chapter Thirteen, Qin Keqing dies — the earliest to perish of the Twelve Beauties of Jinling, her death vague and sudden. Jia Zhen weeps as if he were a fountain of tears, vowing to spend "all that I have" on her funeral. The coffin rests for forty-nine days; one hundred and eighty monks are engaged to chant the Great Compassion Repentance, ninety-nine Taoist priests to perform the Rite of Resolving Grievances and Washing Away Karma. On the day of the funeral procession, the Prince of Dongping, the Commandery Prince of Nan'an, the Prince of Xining, and the Prince of Beijing all set up roadside offering sheds; the Prince of Beijing even came in person. The spatial coordinates of this funeral can be identified almost one by one within Beijing. The Yonghe Temple — the former residence of the Yongzheng Emperor converted into a Tibetan Buddhist monastery — houses a twenty-six-meter sandalwood Maitreya statue in the Pavilion of Ten Thousand Blessings, rising from floor to dome. The immense overpowering sensation of "looking down at the Buddha's feet but unable to see his face" is exactly the spatial effect created by the one hundred and eighty monks chanting in unison over Qin Keqing's bier. That a temple can accommodate such a colossal sutra-chanting retinue is itself evidence of its architectural scale — Jia Zhen's ostentatious "all that I have" can only be understood against the dimensions of the Yonghe Temple. And the Zhihua Temple — the Ming-dynasty family temple of the eunuch Wang Zhen, Director of Ceremonial under the Zhengtong Emperor — conceals an even more secret spatial code. It has preserved intact the full layout of a Ming-dynasty timber building complex, and even more remarkably, its continuously transmitted "Beijing Music," hailed as the living fossil of ancient Chinese music. The harmony of wooden fish, cymbal, pipe, sheng, and flute has resounded in the dim light of the Zhihua Hall for five hundred and sixty years. The sounds of sutra chanting and Sanskrit praise before Qin Keqing's bier — the timbre, the melody, the spatial feel — can be virtually resurrected in the Zhihua Temple's Beijing Music. The funeral procession traveled from the Ningguo Mansion all the way to Iron Threshold Temple. Iron Threshold Temple and Water Moon Convent (Steamed Bun Convent) were the Jia family's private temples — Iron Threshold for the coffin, Steamed Bun Convent for the guests. It was at Steamed Bun Convent that Xifeng abused her authority and Qin Zhong met Zhineng in secret. A strange tension unfolds within the temple space: sutras being chanted on one side, human hearts stirring on the other. On a grander scale, the Ming Xiaoling Mausoleum in Nanjing — the joint burial site of the Ming founder Zhu Yuanzhang and Empress Ma — stretches its spirit-way stone statues nearly two kilometers, the civil and military officials and stone beasts standing in solemn array, making it one of the largest surviving imperial burial complexes in China. The Jia funeral procession, like a "silver mountain pressing down the earth," the roadside offering sheds lined up in a row, the ostentation of the funeral rites — all are essentially the folk-level reduction of the Ming Xiaoling spirit-way ritual system. The roadside offering sheds of princes and ministers were the living-human version of the spirit-way stone statues of an imperial mausoleum. And the Huangshicheng Imperial Archive in Beijing — the Ming and Qing imperial archive, a beamless hall built entirely of stone, designed specifically to house the Yongle Encyclopedia and other state-level documents. What does it have to do with Qin Keqing's funeral? The connection lies in what it represents: the imperial will to "seal important things in indestructible containers." Jia Zhen spent a thousand ounces of silver on a coffin of "ten-thousand-year imperishable" nanmu wood for Qin Keqing, wanting to preserve her beauty forever — while the imperial court, with massive blocks of stone, sealed the memory of an empire. Two kinds of sealing, the same delusion of eternity.
stops.poem:
The Ningguo mansion's funeral shook the capital's ground,
A hundred monks' sutra-chanting filled street and compound.
The stone archive holds old records sealed with care —
But lighter far than one young girl's dream of love's despair.

stops.title: Chapter Seven: The Qingxu Temple Sacrifice · Between Buddha and Dao
stops.content: If Iron Threshold Temple was the solemnity of death, then the Qingxu Temple sacrifice in Chapter Twenty-Nine was the liveliness of the living. The Lady Dowager, with Baoyu, Daiyu, Baochai, Xifeng, and a vast retinue, sets out in full splendor for Qingxu Temple to perform a three-day peace-offering. This is the largest public outing in the entire book — the Lady Dowager's eight-carrier sedan, Aunt Xue's four-carrier sedan, Xifeng's carriage, Daiyu and Baochai sharing a kingfisher-canopied pearl-tasseled eight-treasure carriage, maids and old nurses crammed into the carriages behind — "black and thick, the carriages filled the whole street." What was Qingxu Temple like in reality? There is indeed one in Beijing — now called the White Cloud Temple, the ancestral temple of the Complete Perfection school of Taoism, where the Yuan-dynasty Qiu Chuji once resided, its incense uninterrupted for seven hundred years. Every year from the first to the nineteenth day of the first lunar month, the White Cloud Temple fair draws old Beijingers to "touch the stone monkey," "hit the money bell," and "stroke the bronze beast" — the sea of humanity overlaps almost perfectly with the "black and thick, covering the whole street" of the Lady Dowager's Qingxu Temple expedition. The social details — old Zhang the Taoist exchanging pleasantries with the Lady Dowager, Baoyu's impatience with kneeling and bowing — this worldly social function of a Taoist sanctuary is the very essence of the White Cloud Temple fair. Three days after the Qingxu Temple visit, Baoyu and Daiyu have a terrible quarrel — because Old Zhang proposed a match for Baoyu. One smashes his jade, the other cuts her tassels, throwing the entire household into turmoil. The Lady Dowager cries: "It takes a pair of lovers to make a quarrel." And the entire fuse lay inside that incense-wreathed Taoist temple. In stark contrast to the Taoist temple is the spatial atmosphere of a Buddhist monastery. The White Dagoba of Miaoying Temple in Beijing — designed and built by the Nepalese architect Araniko in the Yuan dynasty — stands pure white, fifty-one meters tall, rising like a white stabilizing pillar from the low-rise residential fabric of old Beijing. The technique of using one solitary, dominating building to command the entire city skyline implies an unshakable spiritual authority. Is there a similar space in Grand View Garden? Yes — Green Bower Hermitage. Indeed, Grand View Garden also contains a nunnery, home to the most singular of the Twelve Beauties of Jinling — Miao-yu. She is a Buddhist nun who still keeps her hair, yet she collects famous ceramic tea wares and is an expert in tea ceremony. In Chapter Forty-One, "Green Bower Hermitage Tastes Plum-Blossom Snow," Miao-yu offers Baochai tea in a rare bao-bao-jia cup, Daiyu tea in a dian-xi-qiao cup, and gives Baoyu her own daily-use green jade vessel. "One cup is for tasting, two cups are for quenching thirst like a brute, three cups are for watering an ox or a donkey." The spatial prototype of Miao-yu's Green Bower Hermitage is not hard to discern. The Wanshou Temple in Beijing's Haidian district — built in the Ming Wanli era, converted to a Tibetan Buddhist monastery in the Qing, and also served as a temporary palace for the Empress Dowager Cixi on her water route to the Summer Palace. A single temple simultaneously carrying three identities: imperial temple, Buddhist hall, and temporary palace. Was not Miao-yu the same? A nun's status, an aristocrat's taste, and a maiden's heart hidden within her plum-blossom snow tea — three identities, one Green Bower Hermitage. The Lingyin Temple Stone Pagodas and Sutra Pillars by West Lake in Hangzhou — survivals from the Five Dynasties Wuyue period, nestled among the lush woods of Peak That Flew Here. The Chan atmosphere of "temple within scenery, scenery within temple" is precisely the landscape key of Miao-yu's Green Bower Hermitage, with its "dozen red plum trees like scattered cinnabar." Even more exquisite is Hangzhou's Baochu Pagoda — the Baochu Pagoda, slender and elegant as a beautiful maiden standing by West Lake, gazing at Leifeng Pagoda across the water. Was not Miao-yu the most solitary pagoda among the Twelve Beauties of Jinling? The others paired off in twos, while she stood alone — but she was a sight to behold. In Dream of the Red Chamber, religion is never monopolized by faith. It is a theater of human affairs, a dark chamber of power exchange, and the last refuge of personal solitude.
stops.poem:
The Taoist altar at Qingxu Temple opened wide,
In Green Bower Hermitage snow-water tea was tried.
The white dagoba stands solitary beyond the cloud —
Miao-yu was the lonely plum, unbowed, unbowed.

stops.title: Chapter Eight: Baoyu Beaten · Officialdom and the Scholar's Path
stops.content: When Jia Zheng's staff came down, the warmest season of Grand View Garden came to an abrupt halt. In Chapter Thirty-Three, a retainer of Prince Zhongshun's mansion arrives demanding the actor Qi Guan, and Jia Huan informs against Baoyu, claiming that Golden's suicide was caused by Baoyu's "attempted rape." Jia Zheng's face turns the color of gold paper. He orders Baoyu pinned to a bench and beaten three or four dozen strokes — "his face pale, his breath weak, the green silk trousers beneath soaked through with blood." Lady Wang rushes in and clings to the staff, crying: "If you must strangle him, get a rope and strangle me first, then strangle him." The Lady Dowager arrives, tottering, and points at Jia Zheng: "I'll take Baoyu and go back to Nanjing this very day!" This is the most intense father-son conflict in Dream of the Red Chamber. The root is not Qi Guan, not Golden — it is the concept Jia Zheng has chanted his whole life: officialdom and the scholar's path. The battlefield of those two men was not on that wooden bench but in a far larger space: the Imperial Academy and the Beijing Confucius Temple. The Imperial Academy was the highest institution of learning for the Yuan, Ming, and Qing dynasties. The Biyong Hall sits at its center — a square structure with double eaves and a pointed roof, surrounded by a moat on four sides, connected to the outside by four white marble bridges. This is where the emperor "ascended the Biyong to lecture." The Qianlong Emperor visited five times, each time crossing the white marble bridges — the majesty of "all nations coming to pay homage" was the kind of order Jia Zheng had pursued his entire life. Flanking the pathways are one hundred and ninety-eight stelae bearing the names of fifty-one thousand six hundred and twenty-four successful metropolitan examination candidates of the Yuan, Ming, and Qing dynasties, each stone soaked with the sweat and tears of countless scholars. When Jia Zheng walked out of the Imperial Academy gate and looked up at the Beijing Confucius Temple next door — the Hall of Great Perfection, nine bays with double eaves, the Kangxi Emperor's "Teacher of Ten Thousand Generations" plaque imposing in its dignity — you can imagine his state of mind: Your great-grandmother was the Kangxi Emperor's wet nurse, your grandfather Cao Yin was the literary leader of the Jiangnan elite, but your generation — no inherited title, no examination degree, scraping by as a minor functionary in the Ministry of Works only through "imperial grace." He placed the ideals he could never realize on his son Baoyu's shoulders. But Baoyu would have none of it. He called those who thirsted for official honors "grain moths" — worms in the rice-bin of officialdom. He called the eight-legged essay books "those books the ancients wrote when they had nothing better to do — all that moralizing and fine phrases, originally meant to mislead future generations of bewhiskered dolts." He only wanted to stay in the garden with Daiyu, read The Western Chamber, watch the falling blossoms, and speak a few wild words. Years later, when you pass the Imperial Academy gates and gaze a little longer at those examination stelae — you understand Jia Zheng's despair. The humiliation of knowing that "the entire society's ladder of advancement is right there, and your son will not even look at it" — that hurts far more than thirty or forty strokes of the staff. But the Jia family was not only about Jia Zheng. There was also Baoyu's great-grandfather, Jia Daishan, the Lady Dowager's husband, who had risen through military merit. The founders of the Jia clan, the Duke of Ningguo and the Duke of Rongguo, had won the family estate fighting alongside the founding emperor. This is why the novel repeatedly mentions "hunting at Iron Net Mountain" — Jia Zhen and Jia Rong leading their men into the mountains for days of hunting. This martial tradition of the Manchu aristocracy has a coordinate in real space: The Altar of Agriculture — where Ming and Qing emperors sacrificed to the God of Agriculture and performed the plowing ceremony. The Hall of the Year Star, the Observation Platform, the sacred three-fen plot where the emperor personally grasped the plow and walked three rounds to demonstrate "agriculture first." What does this have to do with "hunting at Iron Net Mountain"? The connection is this: the Altar of Agriculture represents a path within the orthodox system that does not rely on examinations — the path of farming and military service. The Jia ancestors took the military path; by Jia Zheng's generation, the clan had been forced to turn toward the examination system. The pain of this transition was projected directly onto Baoyu: you not only refuse to study the martial arts — you won't even study your books properly? After Baoyu's beating, Daiyu came to see him. Her eyes were "swollen like peaches, her face covered with tears." She managed only half a sentence: "You — you had better change your ways from now on." Baoyu never changed. He would never change. He was that stone Nüwa had left behind — not good enough to patch the heavens, too proud to pursue official honors, too disdainful for the examination life. He would rather be beaten, rather be a good-for-nothing, rather spend his whole life among girls — than become the kind of man his father wanted him to be. "Unfit to patch the azure sky, In vain I drifted through the mortal world for many a year." — The verdict written in the very first chapter of the book. Not Lin Daiyu's verdict. Jia Baoyu's.
stops.poem:
Beside the Biyong's moat the examination rolls are kept,
Fifty thousand scholars' names in marble deeply wept.
At Iron Net Mountain the forebears hunted wide and far,
And under the staff the rejected stone cried out — a scar.

stops.title: Chapter Nine: The Mid-Autumn Feast · Linked Verses at Concave Crystal Lodge
stops.content: Chapters Seventy-Five and Seventy-Six contain the ultimate Mid-Autumn scene in the entire book. It may be the finest Mid-Autumn Festival in all of classical Chinese literature. That afternoon, Jia Zhen and his concubines are enjoying the moonlight in the Ningguo Mansion when they hear a sigh coming from the ancestral hall — a sinister, ill-omened sound. That evening, the Lady Dowager hosts a family banquet at Convex Emerald Hall in Grand View Garden — "all the tables and chairs were round, to symbolize reunion." Yet the atmosphere is colder than ever: Xifeng is ill and absent, Baochai has moved back to her own home for the holiday, and Li Wan has also pleaded illness. The lively crowds of past years are gone; only a handful remain. Even the Lady Dowager says: "In years gone by, at this hour, we would have thirty or forty people, men and women — how lively it was! Tonight — so few." After the banquet, Daiyu and Xiangyun linger. The two girls slip away to Concave Crystal Lodge — a waterside open pavilion where the moonlight ripples on the water. There they compose linked verses, from "On this night of the Mid-Autumn Festival" all the way to "A chilled pond reflects the crane's shadow, cold moonlight buries the flower's soul." "Cold moonlight buries the flower's soul" — no sooner are these five words out than Miao-yu emerges from the shadows and interrupts them. "Fine verses, fine verses," she says, "but too desolate, too sad. It touches on one's fate." Then she takes them to Green Bower Hermitage for tea. This Mid-Autumn garden atmosphere finds echoes in several real spaces. The Zhan Garden in Nanjing, the Ming-dynasty garden of Prince Zhongshan Xu Da, is hailed as "the finest garden of Jinling." Its essence lies in a crescent of clear water — pavilions and terraces built along the shore, the shimmering interplay of light and reflection on the water under moonlight. The scene of Daiyu and Xiangyun composing verses by the waterside at Concave Crystal Lodge — moonlight falling on the water, their poems scattering in the breeze — captures the most moving instant of a moonlit night at Zhan Garden's waterside pavilion. The garden technique of taking water as a mirror and the moon as a soul is the most poetic spatial language of Jiangnan gardens. The Wenlan Pavilion by West Lake in Hangzhou — one of the seven great libraries of the Qing-dynasty Complete Library of the Four Treasuries, and the only surviving one of the three Jiangnan libraries. Outside the pavilion is a pond, rockeries, and covered walkways — a space where scholars could pace along the water's edge, composing poems under the moonlight. The waterside space outside this library has precisely the character of Concave Crystal Lodge: the muse flows by the water's edge. Concave Crystal Lodge held no books, but Daiyu and Xiangyun both carried a bellyful of poetry. The mooncakes were eaten, the opera ended, the crowd dispersed. Daiyu and Xiangyun sat side by side at the water's edge, linking verses, then falling silent. The most stunning line in the entire book was born from this silence: "A chilled pond reflects the crane's shadow, cold moonlight buries the flower's soul." After this Mid-Autumn Festival, Cao Xueqin never allowed the Jia family to reunite again. When that moon set, the sun of the Jia house set with it.
stops.poem:
At Convex Emerald Hall the fading moonlight falls,
Beyond Concave Crystal Lodge the cold water calls.
Their linked verse died in desolation's throat —
By Zhan Garden's pond a single crane's shadow floats.

stops.title: Chapter Ten: The Raid on Grand View Garden · Qingwen Banished
stops.content: The turning point of Grand View Garden comes in Chapter Seventy-Four. The cause is an embroidered love pouch — picked up by Foolish Sister behind the rockeries of Grand View Garden. Lady Wang's fury blazes: she orders Xifeng and a team of stewardesses to conduct a night raid, turning every room upside down, searching for "indecent objects." This is the famous "Raid on Grand View Garden" — the darkest scene in the entire novel. Overnight, Siqi is expelled (love letters and shoes from her cousin are found), Ruhua is expelled (items deposited by her brother are discovered), and Qingwen is expelled — though nothing incriminating is found on her, Lady Wang dislikes her "eyebrows that look like Daiyu's" and calls her "that妖精-like creature," dragging her from her sickbed and throwing her out. Tanchun is the most fierce. She had foreseen this night. When Xifeng and her party arrive at Autumn Freshness Studio, Tanchun "stood by a candle with the door wide open" — she sits in the middle of the room, all her trunks and chests open, and says icily: "Don't rush — your own turn to be searched will come soon enough. Don't you know that great families, if attacked from outside, cannot be killed all at once? The ancients said: 'A millipede may die but never stiffens.' It is only when the killing begins within the house itself that total ruin follows." The spatial language of this scene deserves close reading. Prince Gong's Mansion — the Prince Gong's Mansion and Garden — seven courtyards deep, one after another, the deeper you go, the more oppressive it becomes. When Xifeng and the lantern-bearing stewardesses passed through one festooned gate after another, one covered corridor after another, the spatial "step-by-step closing in" is precisely the rhythm of the raid on Grand View Garden. The sisters of Grand View Garden had all walked this path before — but then it was to admire flowers; this time, it was to tear down their home. From an architectural-spatial perspective, the raid on Grand View Garden carries a deeper metaphor: the Forbidden City's seventy-two hectares of forbidden precincts have also known "raids" — the confiscation of Heshen's estate, the seizure of Su Shun's property, countless officials swallowed by political vortexes. Prince Gong's Mansion was itself formerly Heshen's residence; after Heshen was ordered to commit suicide by the Jiaqing Emperor, the mansion was raided. Grand View Garden was the Jia family's private garden; Prince Gong's Mansion was the Qing state's official residence — but the raid's route, its spatial feeling, is identical: deep night, lanterns, trunks overturned, cries and weeping — along those same covered corridors that once hung with red lanterns now rolled the footsteps of the confiscation party. After Qingwen was thrown out of Grand View Garden, Baoyu sneaked out to see her. She lay on a broken-down kang in her cousin's house, covered with an old quilt, her throat burning with thirst, unable even to get a drink of water. She bit off her own fingernails, took off the red silk jacket she wore next to her skin — and gave them to Baoyu. That night, Qingwen died. Baoyu wrote the "Elegy for the Lotus Maid" to mourn her: "So fragile the flower, how could it withstand the gale? So sorrowful the willow, how endure the sudden storm?" After the raid, the soul of Grand View Garden dissipated. The bamboos of Bamboo Lodge never rustled again. The strange herbs of Alpinia Park lost their fragrance. The crabapple of Happy Red Court withered by half. When Yuanchun made her homecoming visit, the Jia family had spent hundreds of thousands of silver taels to build this garden. No one imagined — before it had even been occupied ten years — it would be dismantled from within by its own people.
stops.poem:
The raiders' lanterns lit the covered walkway's gloom,
Tanchun by candle cursed the madness and the doom.
At Prince Gong's Mansion, all the heavy gates are sealed —
From that night on, the garden stood empty, grass revealed.

stops.title: Chapter Eleven: The Old Dream of Jinling · The Red Chamber Broken
stops.content: In the final chapters of Dream of the Red Chamber, the pace abruptly quickens. It is as if Cao Xueqin could no longer bear to continue writing — Yuanchun dies suddenly, Wang Ziteng dies violently, Lin Daiyu burns her manuscripts to sever her infatuation, Xue Baochai dons her bridal finery to complete her great ritual — nearly every chapter claims someone's life. In Chapter One Hundred and Five, it finally comes — the Imperial Guard raids and confiscates the Ningguo Mansion. Jia She is arrested, Jia Lian is taken away, Xifeng faints on the spot. This is no slow slide between life and death, between honor and disgrace — it is a single thunderous crash. And it is precisely the artistic reenactment of Cao Xueqin's own family fate — during the Yongzheng reign, the Cao household was raided, its property confiscated, the entire family escorted under guard back to Beijing. Qinhuai, Jinling — the ancestral home of the Jia family — all its glory turned to ruins. The old Cao family mansion in Jinling that Cao Xueqin wrote of finds its real-world counterpart in the Ming Palace Ruins. The Ming Palace was the magnificent imperial city built by Zhu Yuanzhang in Nanjing: Meridian Gate, Gate of Supreme Harmony, Hall of Supreme Harmony, Canopy Hall, Hall of Solemnity — its central axis over a kilometer long, vaster and more magnificent than the later Forbidden City in Beijing. Today, nothing remains above ground but stone plinths and fragmentary walls. But walking along that central axis in Xuanwu District, you can still feel an immense emptiness. It is like standing before the ruined Jia mansion, imagining the days of "white jade for halls, gold for horses." When Cao Xueqin wrote "mean hovels and empty halls, once piled with official tablets; withered grass and decaying willows, once a theater of song and dance" — these sixteen words speak not of others but of the Cao family, and of the Ming Palace. But the empire's map extends beyond Jinling and the capital. The novel mentions "hunting at Iron Net Mountain" several times — Jia Zhen and Jia Rong taking men into the mountains for days of hunting. It is not that a real palace stood on Iron Net Mountain, but in the Qing imperial geography, there was indeed such a place — the Mountain Resort in Chengde. Covering five hundred and sixty-four hectares, the Chengde Mountain Resort is twice the size of the Summer Palace and eight times the size of Beihai. Three landscape types — lakes, plains, and mountains — were arranged to mirror the Chinese empire: the southeastern lake district imitates the Jiangnan water country, the northwestern plain imitates the Mongolian grasslands, while the northern section is a natural imperial hunting ground. Every summer, the Kangxi and Qianlong emperors came here to escape the heat, hunt, and conduct state affairs. On the hunting grounds, fine horses neighed and arrows split the air; in the resort, memorials traveled back and forth and envoys came to court. The casually mentioned "hunting at Iron Net Mountain" on Jia Zhen's lips, scaled to the Mountain Resort, becomes an imperial spirit contending with heaven and earth. Near the resort stands a singular temple — the Temple of the Potaraka Doctrine. Modeled on the Potala Palace in Tibet, its Great Red Terrace rises twenty-five meters, seven rows of windows densely arrayed on its red granite surface. Here the Qianlong Emperor received Mongol princes and Tibetan Living Buddhas — the cultures of Han, Tibetan, Mongol, and Manchu converged before this temple. Dream of the Red Chamber does not explicitly name it — but the imperial map it helped shape was the entire political ecology upon which the Jia family rested. After Yuanchun's death in the palace, the red walls of this temple seemed to stand silent in the distance — knowing that this empire, for all its seeming solidity, had long had grasses growing through the cracks between the bricks of the Four Great Families. The book's final scene is Jia Baoyu's departure. Transformed by the monk and the priest, he bows three times from afar to Jia Zheng in the snow at Piling Station — then vanishes into the vast white expanse. Jia Zheng chases after him, calling his name, but sees only "a boundless white wilderness — not a single soul." That passage has made countless readers weep: "My dwelling is on the Ridge of Blue Ridge Peak. My travels take me through the chaos of the primal void. Who shall wander with me? Whom shall I follow? Vast and boundless — I return to the Great Waste." Snow falls, flake by flake, on that stone left behind when the heavens were mended. It is the ruin of Grand View Garden. It is the stone plinth of the Ming Palace. It is the broken wall of Yuanmingyuan. It is the Cao family's old house after the raid. It is every shattered dream of Chinese architecture. And the Yuanmingyuan Ruins — the ruin of the Garden of Ten Thousand Gardens — those fire-scorched white marble columns slanting in the wild grass suggest the smashed potted landscapes of Grand View Garden. In the Tongzhi reign, an attempt was made to rebuild it, but the nation's strength had declined and timber was insufficient, so the effort fizzled — just as the Jia family dreamed of a revival "like flowers trimmed with brocade and a roaring fire under the cauldron," only to end in nothing. The greatest ruined garden and the greatest novel of a ruined family gaze at each other in silence across time. Step out of the Yuanmingyuan Ruins Park gate, stand on West Qinghua Road, and look back — those broken walls and shattered pillars become silhouettes against the setting sun. And suddenly you understand the opening of Dream of the Red Chamber: "This is the first chapter. The author says: Having once passed through a dream, I therefore concealed the true events and, borrowing the language of spiritual understanding, wrote this book, The Story of the Stone." This is not fiction. It is what one city, one family, one dynasty spent centuries building and then destroying — which Cao Xueqin, in the name of a single stone, preserved on paper.
stops.poem:
In Jinling the old palace walls decay in fading light,
At Chengde Mountain Resort the hunt fires burn low in night.
The Red Chamber stones can never all be swept away —
Under Yuanmingyuan's lingering snow, homeward shadows stray.
